To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ECP is a multitask protein with a wide range antimicrobial activity that is mainly based on the protein interaction with the Gram-negative bacterial wall, and that the ECP activity requires the presence of a cluster of basic residues at the protein surface.

the structural determinants of the antimicrobial activity of the eosinophils RNase 3 are the cationic surface patches, which interact with the bacterial surface, and the active site, which interacts with nucleic acids.

(i) the ECP activity is mainly due to its interaction with the lipids of the outer membrane; (ii) a direct mechanical action on the bacteria wall is sufficient to kill the bacteria, while the protein may also act intracellularly; (iii) a specific sequence motif, including the cationic residues of the ECP surface, is essential for the biological activity; (iv) the ECP structure is a prototype for the design of antimicrobial peptides.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the structure-function relationships of the ECP antimicrobial activity.
the elucidation of structural determinants of the ECP activity, with the aim to understand the molecular mechanism of action and the role of this protein in the host defence.

the structural determinants of ECP activity, with the aim to provide a general framework to understand the antimicrobial activity of RNases and to identify the protein residues that can be used to design new antimicrobial agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ECP activity is a result of the combination of a series of non-covalent interactions between protein and bacterial targets, which are finely tuned by the protein structure.

RNases have been selected for their intrinsic ability to interact with nucleotides and anionic polysaccharides, and that their antibacterial action has been evolved as a side effect of this interaction, rather than as a direct target of their enzymatic activity.
the RNase A super family evolved from an ancient defence protein and, although the catalytic site was maintained, the protein acquired a variety of new functions, such as the antibacterial action.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ECP is a versatile protein with a broad range of biological activities that may have been selected in evolution to cope with different pathogens.
the protein structure, although not optimized for catalysis, is finely tuned to interact with anionic bacterial targets, providing an efficient antimicrobial activity.
a single protein, by means of its surface charge distribution, is able to bind to different anionic targets with high affinity and specificity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of experimental and computational approaches is required to provide a comprehensive picture of the protein function and to define the key residues for the protein activity.
a combination of structure-based computational and biochemical approaches can be successfully exploited for the design and development of new antimicrobial drugs.
the ECP activity is not a unique feature of this protein, but it is a general property of the RNase A family.
